title: 曾名 Coda 的 Superhuman Docs 与 Notion：哪个更好？[2026] | Zapier
author: Ryan Kane
content:
I've been using Notion to take notes and organize my life for a few years now. As you might expect with a popular app like Notion, there are quite a few alternatives these days. Superhuman Docs (formerly known as Coda) might be the clearest 1:1 substitute for Notion if you're looking to try something new.

I compared Notion against Coda for a prior version of this article. A lot has changed since then: Coda is now part of a larger suite of connected workspace apps under the Superhuman brand. In some ways, the shift to Superhuman Docs is a straightforward rebrand, but in others—particularly as it relates to AI—the app is now far more capable than it used to be.

Turn ideas into action
Automate your note-taking

To compare Notion and Superhuman Docs and figure out what each app is best at, I got hands-on with the latest features. Here's what I discovered—and how to decide which is right for you.

Table of contents:

  • Notion vs. Superhuman Docs at a glance

  • Notion offers more flexibility; Superhuman Docs scales better for teams

  • Notion is better for text and note-taking; Superhuman Docs is better for data management

  • Notion's desktop and mobile apps are more refined and include offline mode

  • Notion's AI includes autonomous agents; Superhuman Docs offers AI on all paid plans

  • Notion has a thriving user community; Superhuman Docs provides expert-led trainings

  • Superhuman Docs is more cost-effective for teams

  • Superhuman Docs has more app integrations, but both connect to Zapier

  • Superhuman Docs vs. Notion: Which should you use?

Notion vs. Superhuman Docs at a glance

Superhuman Docs and Notion are similar apps, and they even look pretty much the same. They do have differences, though. Broadly speaking, Notion is great at documents and wikis, well-suited for individual users and small teams, and has AI agents that can work on their own; Superhuman Docs is better-suited to data work, scales better for large organizations, and is more affordable if you're adding lots of users.

Here's a quick summary, but keep reading for a more detailed breakdown.

Superhuman Docs

Notion

Ease of use and features

⭐⭐⭐⭐ Intuitive but less flexible and comes with a slight learning curve; far fewer templates, but Docs AI can fill in the gaps

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Easy to set up and intuitive to use; 30,000+ templates

Databases

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Advanced tables and databases with easy-to-use formulas; ability to sync table data across docs

⭐⭐⭐⭐ Powerful tables and databases; basic data management features

Collaboration

⭐⭐⭐⭐ Real-time collaboration with unlimited editors; users on free plans can't share docs above a certain size

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Real-time collaboration; limited to 10 guests on a free account

AI features

⭐⭐⭐⭐ Docs AI builds tables, views, and content inside your documents; included on every paid plan

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Notion AI comes with agentic capabilities that let you outsource multi-step projects rather than just one-off tasks

Mobile apps and offline access

⭐⭐⭐ Native macOS, iOS, and Android apps (Windows app is coming soon); you can keep editing the page you're on if your connection drops, but you can't download pages ahead of time

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Highly rated desktop and mobile apps for all major platforms; offline mode lets you download pages ahead of time

Community and support

⭐⭐⭐ Community is much smaller than Notion's; webinars and trainings on every plan, with group trainings on Business

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Strong community following with a variety of community-hosted events and endless templates, groups, and forums

Pricing

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Paid plans start at $12/user/month, billed annually; Business plan is $33/user/month; only Doc Makers pay for seats (Editors are free); all paid plans include AI and access to other Superhuman apps

⭐⭐⭐⭐ Paid plans start at $10/user/month, billed annually; Notion AI requires the $20/user/month Business plan; fantastic free plan for individual users

Integrations

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Over 800 available; integrates with Zapier; MCP server

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Over 500 available; integrates with Zapier; MCP server

Notion offers more flexibility and a quicker learning curve; Superhuman Docs scales better for teams

Notion is known for being intuitive to use and easy to set up. Once you create an account, you'll also have access to their Getting Started document, which gives you an easy-to-digest rundown of the basics. From there, the app does a good job of guiding you through the rest of its block-based editor as you use it.

Whether you want to set up a complex project management system or—like me—a simple home base for organizing work and personal projects, Notion makes it easy.

Notion's sidebar and dashboards make it intuitive to jump between pages and subpages and organize everything visually. I tend to keep things simple rather than tinker too much with dashboards and productivity systems, but I'm probably in the minority judging by the 30,000+ Notion templates you can install to track your goals, set up to-do lists, and create a "Personal HQ" (like the below template) to organize all the day-to-day details of your life.

Notion is also incredibly flexible. For example, say you're creating a simple database comparing travel destinations. Both Notion and Superhuman Docs let you enrich each row with notes, but Notion also turns each row into an infinitely expandable page of its own. Like a workspace version of Inception, you can create databases that contain pages, then put databases and subpages within those pages, and so on until you're satisfied.

If you're used to Notion, the first thing you'll notice about Superhuman Docs is that it takes hierarchy more seriously. Rather than a pages-within-pages free-for-all, Superhuman Docs is more similar to a traditional file system: workspaces contain folders and folders contain docs.

Once you're inside a doc, you can add pages and subpages, all of which show up cleanly on the sidebar. Within your pages, you'll see subpages show up as big buttons right under the header—rather than embedded randomly throughout the document, as is often the case in Notion.

Superhuman Docs' interface presents some minor downsides for solo users. It feels more rigid than Notion, and it's harder to jump between everything in your workspace within a single view.

But those same qualities also make Superhuman Docs better for many team use cases. Navigating a Notion workspace with a half-dozen (or more) layers of randomly embedded subpages can make it challenging to find what you need, especially if you're onboarding new team members. With Superhuman Docs, you can reduce that overwhelm by setting up each doc as a focused workspace for individual teams or projects. On the Business plan, you can also add subfolders and private folders for specific teams.

Because of Superhuman Docs' relative lack of templates, you'll probably need to learn it by building from scratch rather than importing templates and tweaking settings. Superhuman Docs does have some templates, but they're mostly for narrow use cases (like this Kanban board below) rather than fully-realized dashboards, hubs, or systems. That's less of a hurdle than it used to be, though, now that AI can create dashboards from a prompt. (More on each app's AI capabilities shortly.)

Notion offers a staggering 30,000+ free and paid templates, including 4,000+ in its "Planning and Goals" category alone. If you want to create an entire workspace for your company in one click—including a team wiki, projects hub, content calendar, and CRM—Notion has dozens of company hub templates that let you start with something prebuilt and customize it.

Notion is better for text and note-taking; Superhuman Docs is better for data management

Turn your Notion workspace into an information hub
Automate Notion

I use Notion every day to organize research and write long-form content, and what I most appreciate is that it empowers me to create a messy, random set of notes that fits my workflow perfectly. First and foremost is Notion's infinite page nesting, which is especially handy for research. I'll often go at least three levels deep with nested subpages, especially if I'm pulling from lots of sources and need to keep things easy to browse.

With Notion, you can also add those nested subpages anywhere while you write or edit, making it easy to create dynamic documents that let you access the information you need without making things too crowded. Superhuman Docs allows infinite subpages too, but since they're automatically grouped at the top of your document, they lose important context.

You can also achieve this a bit more elegantly with toggles. Superhuman Docs can do toggles too, but Notion lets you infinitely nest toggles within toggles, while Superhuman Docs doesn't.

Superhuman Docs, meanwhile, is a more capable tool if you're dealing with lots of data and want lots of options for organizing and displaying it. While tables in both apps seem quite similar visually, they have some meaningful differences in terms of functionality.

Here's an example of a project management chart in Notion.

And here's a similar one in Superhuman Docs, including advanced features like voting systems and progress trackers.

Superhuman Docs is slightly more intuitive for formulas if you're doing them manually. Its interface works more or less like a spreadsheet app, and it isn't intimidating for non-technical users. But if you have access to Docs AI, you should absolutely use that, since you can just describe what you need instead of fiddling around with variables.

Notion also lets you add formulas without dealing with code. It's not quite as intuitive as Superhuman Docs if you're fine-tuning things manually, mainly because Notion's "Edit formula" menu can be overwhelming. But AI helps here, too: as long as you're on the Notion Business plan, you can just ask Notion Agent to build whatever formulas you need.

Notion's desktop and mobile experiences are more refined and include offline mode

Notion's apps are available across all major desktop and mobile platforms, including macOS, Windows, Android, and iOS. You can also access it from a web browser and use Notion's clipper extension to save web pages to your workspace.

If you're like me and do almost all of your work in a browser these days, desktop apps might not normally factor into your decision-making process. But Notion's desktop and mobile apps both include offline mode, which is a big deal for an app that aims to be your workspace for everything.

Offline mode is implemented in a clever way: in addition to toggling it on for individual documents, you can also ask Notion to automatically download all of your recently modified docs. This makes it much more likely you'll actually be able to access your projects when you open your laptop on a flight or in a cafe with terrible Wi-Fi.

Superhuman Docs doesn't offer a proper offline mode, which leads to some clumsy workarounds, as one consultant reported: "I train all my clients to keep their main document open on their laptops at all times, and to hibernate their laptop instead of shutting down… this way, they always have their main doc up and running, even if they have no internet connection."

While Superhuman Docs' web app offers a polished experience, its iOS and Android mobile apps are weaker, with many users complaining about sign-in issues, laggy performance, missing features—and no offline mode.

Notion's AI includes autonomous agents; Superhuman Docs offers AI on every paid plan

I tested the latest versions of Notion AI and Superhuman's "Docs AI," and they're both really, really good. Gone are the days when these AI assistants were basically just question-and-answer engines. Now, they'll actually build stuff for you within your workspace. As a result, templates and other usability aids aren't quite as relevant anymore, because Notion and Superhuman Docs are quite capable of using AI to build whatever you ask for.

One eye-opening moment I had while testing was realizing that I could build a fully-functional project tracker from scratch just by dragging a screenshot into the chat window and saying "build something like this." Both Notion AI and Docs AI were able to fully recreate what I wanted, including adding dummy data (and in some cases improving upon my original request). Here's what that looked like in Superhuman Docs.

Notion AI could already do this sort of thing, but it's a big deal for Docs AI, which used to focus on answering questions, drafting text, and adding data to tables. Now, Docs AI can create databases and project trackers, bulk-update rows, add kanban or timeline views, pull data from a folder of PDF invoices, or reply to comments. It's also context-aware, so if you have relevant information elsewhere in your workspace, Docs AI can take that into account.

The old table-level AI tools are still around, too. AI columns, which work a bit like Airtable field agents, let you populate each row using AI. You can embed column-level actions that generate summaries or sentiment evaluations, or automatically flag urgency based on a task's due date and status.

Superhuman Docs also includes AI views, a vibe-coding tool that lets you make interactive apps using the data in your docs. Notion does something similar, but it creates web apps that are separate from the rest of the Notion experience. With Superhuman Docs, it's all integrated: you can easily toggle back and forth from table view to your interactive app without leaving your workspace.

Just keep in mind that you need to have a paid seat to use Docs AI. If you have an Editor seat, you'll get access to a limited trial, but you're still restricted from certain actions.

Notion AI does nearly everything that Docs AI does, but it goes further in a few areas. It can also:

  • Search across multiple connected apps, like Slack and Google Drive

  • Take action across your Notion workspace, rather than just the doc you're currently looking at

  • Let you choose between AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google

  • Record your meetings and create transcripts with action items (Superhuman recently acquired Fathom, an AI notetaker, and plans to add this feature too)

  • Run Custom Agents that work autonomously

If you're looking for an AI teammate that can handle ongoing tasks within your workspace, only Notion is set up for that. Notion's Custom Agents can handle entire workflows on their own.

Notion's 150+ custom agent templates include a Task Triage Agent, an Auto-Updating FAQ Agent, a Project Manager, and an Agency Operations Manager. (One of the most popular agents is, perhaps inevitably, the Notion Agent Builder.) Or you can skip the templates altogether and just ask your Notion Agent to build a custom agent for you.

The idea is to identify busywork, assign those tasks to Custom Agents, and have them handle the workflows moving forward. You can even create teams of specialized agents that hand off jobs to one another.

Notion AI requires the Business plan, which costs $20/user/month, billed annually. (If you're on the Free or Plus plan, you'll get a limited trial.) As of November 2026, Notion meters your AI usage with credits. Each user gets 1,500 credits for standard tasks and 500 credits for specialized tasks, like Custom Agents. A task might cost anywhere from 5-150 credits, depending on the complexity of your project and the AI model you're using.

Notion has a thriving user community; Superhuman Docs provides expert-led trainings

Notion has an unusually fanatical user following. You can find Notion community groups on every continent except Antarctica, a fan-created swag shop that sells Notion-branded hoodies and socks, and dozens of monthly in-person events around the world (including one cozy-sounding event in Montana titled "Notion Newbie Tea Time").

Whenever apps have this level of enthusiasm, it's a good sign that the team is highly engaged with users and incorporates their feedback to improve the product. In Notion's case, it also means you can find answers to any questions you have relatively quickly via Notion's communities on Reddit, Discord, Facebook, LinkedIn, and elsewhere.

Superhuman Docs' user community is far less active. Its subreddit, for example, only gets a couple of posts per month, compared with 1,300 contributions per week on Notion's subreddit. If you're looking for expert-led training and support, though, Superhuman Docs has options: Business users get access to group trainings and priority support, while Enterprise users get an assigned customer success manager and private trainings. There are also frequent webinars and trainings that anyone can join, even if you're on the free plan.

Superhuman Docs is more cost-effective for most teams

At first glance, Notion seems more affordable than Superhuman Docs, and in some scenarios, it is. But it's not always so black and white.

Notion's Plus plan costs $10/user/month and Superhuman Docs' Pro plan costs $12/user/month, both billed annually. To upgrade from there, you'll pay $20/user/month for Notion Business, or $33/user/month for Superhuman Docs Business.

Despite Superhuman Docs' higher per-seat price, it's often cheaper for teams since you only pay for "Doc Makers" (users who create docs or pages, or use Docs AI). Editors can collaborate for free. With Notion, every workspace user needs to pay for a seat, even if they're just leaving comments.

As one Reddit user explained, "My org has six users but only one doc creator, so I pay for one account." A team of six people—one Doc Maker and five Editors—on Superhuman's Pro plan would pay just $12/month instead of $60/month on Notion's Plus plan.

Just keep in mind that even if you intend to stick to a free Editor role in Superhuman Docs, it's easy to end up with a paid seat by accident. All it takes is completing a "Doc Maker action," which in most cases is triggered as soon as you create a new doc or page. It only took me about 15 minutes of testing before getting an email that I had automatically been upgraded to a Doc Maker seat—so you'll need to keep a close eye on your team's roles to avoid surprise charges.

Superhuman also gives you access to a broader set of workspace apps. Every paid Superhuman plan gives you access to Superhuman Docs, Grammarly, and Superhuman Go (an AI assistant). Superhuman's $33/user/month Business plan also gives your team access to Superhuman Mail.

Note: You can invite guests to review Notion documents for free, but they can only access the individual pages you invite them to, not the whole workspace.

Both apps also offer a free plan. I have a soft spot for Notion's free plan, having used it for years as a personal workspace without running into issues. (Though the 5MB file upload limit on the free plan is a bit of a buzzkill.) Superhuman Docs' free plan lets you add 10MB files, which is nice. But it sets confusing limits on the sort of pages you can share: they can't have more than 50 objects or 1,000 rows per doc. That said, if you're not sharing docs with other people and just need a free personal workspace, you'll likely have a similar experience with either app.

Superhuman Docs has more integrations, but both apps connect to Zapier

Superhuman Docs offers over 800 app integrations, while Notion lists a little over 500.

You may need to upgrade your plan to get the integrations you need, though, since both Notion and Superhuman Docs tier integration access by plan. Entry-level paid plans include basic apps, business plans add more, and enterprise plans include everything.

Both apps also offer an MCP server, so you can connect AI tools like Claude or ChatGPT and have them interact with your workspace directly. You'll probably need to budget for a Superhuman Pro plan or a Notion Business plan if you want to use MCP, since the free plans have usage restrictions.

Both Superhuman Docs and Notion also connect to Zapier, so you can connect them with thousands of other apps to fill any gaps. Once you've connected your apps, you can automate daily tasks like adding new calendar events or form responses to your database. Superhuman Docs vs. Notion: Which should you use?

Notion is often touted as the most flexible tool for individual users and small teams, and after my testing, that feels true for me too. As a solo user who just needs a workspace for research, writing, and light project management, I found Notion to be easier to mold to my needs.

But if you have a larger team, Superhuman Docs' advantages start to come into play—particularly its pricing model and its ability to more rigidly separate projects and teams. And unless you need autonomous agents, the latest version of its AI assistant is now nearly on par with Notion's.

Here's a quick recap of how to decide which app makes sense for you.

Choose Notion if:

  • You're an individual user or a small team

  • You need a tool that's easy to set up and use

  • You want AI agents that can handle recurring work on their own

  • You want your entire team to have AI and document-making capabilities

  • You want solid offline access on desktop and mobile

Choose Superhuman Docs if:

  • You're a large or scaling organization

  • You need the app for data management and automation, not just text

  • You're willing to navigate a slightly longer learning curve

  • You want to create clear project or team-based guardrails within your workspace

  • You want AI access on every paid plan, and you want to reduce costs by keeping certain users in free Editor roles

  • You want Grammarly, Superhuman's AI assistant, and Superhuman Mail bundled into the same subscription

mainPoints.explanation: Notion 以直观的界面和丰富的模板库著称，让用户能够快速搭建复杂的系统。Superhuman Docs 的灵活性稍逊，但结构更清晰，在大型团队和数据密集型项目中更容易扩展。
在处理大型数据集方面，Superhuman Docs 优于 Notion：它提供更强大的表格功能、高级公式，以及与外部数据源更好的集成能力。Notion 的表格足以满足基本需求，但功能深度不及 Superhuman Docs。
两个平台都配备了出色的 AI 助手，但用途不同。Notion AI 侧重于能够自主处理多步骤任务的智能体，而 Docs AI 更擅长在工作空间内解读和处理数据。

keyQuotes: Notion 擅长文档和维基，适合个人用户和小型团队，而且拥有能够自主工作的 AI 智能体；Superhuman Docs 则更适合数据工作，在大型组织中更容易扩展，并且在增加大量用户时更实惠。
如果手动编写公式，Superhuman Docs 的公式功能用起来稍微更直观。它的界面基本上像电子表格应用，对非技术用户来说也不会让人望而生畏。
Notion 的桌面端和移动端应用都支持离线模式。对于一款旨在成为全能工作空间的应用来说，这一点非常重要。
